subjects.displayTitle: Poetry and quoted verse: longing, consolation, and the life of words
subjects.introduction: Which city is the most pleasant? The one where the beloved lives, answers the lover, and poetry’s whole claim on the spirit is in that reply. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, worn out, glances at a letter naming distant friends, finds his weariness turned to joy, and reaches at once for Sa‘dí: whence comes this minstrel who has named my Friend? Verse, he tells a young poet, is sweeter and more penetrating than prose; but praise without inner meaning is glass without a lamp, a body without a soul. Roses and nightingales, wine and tress, the torn garment of separation move through letters, elegies and remembered conversations, and a familiar couplet changes its work with each use, consoling the bereaved, urging patience, redirecting praise toward service. The springtime call of the Song of Songs to rise and come away, with its longing for the beloved’s voice, listens alongside. The path leads on into the mystical themes these poems carry and into the stories and anecdotes in which such lines were first spoken.
subjects.arc: Begin with the beloved’s presence and the power of a voice; explore poetic craft, awakening and joy; enter longing and trial, then return through consolation to service and renewed fellowship.

order.why: Enter the poem of raining mysteries and fragrant wind.
Open with the surprising answer to what makes a city pleasant.
shortened:
A beloved one said to a lover, "O youth!
You have seen many cities in your travels -
Which of those cities is the most pleasant?"
He replied, "That city wherein dwells the beloved."

order.why: Show a familiar verse changing exhaustion into joy.
Let the mention of a name move both speaker and hearer.
Introduce the reported image of speaking through love without lips.
shortened: There is another poem in Persian which says, of a lover speaking with his beloved: "I am speaking to you now without using my lips. I am speaking to you through my love." This is the spiritual language, the language of the Kingdom of GOD.

order.why: Invite the reader to hear the tale through symbols and allusions.
Explore the stated power of verse to carry meanings.
Name the revealing of inner meaning as a purpose of composition.
Connect pearl-like verses with striving and perseverance.
Ask how words, meaning and lived reality belong together.
Consider the text’s distinction between the scope of different poetic effects.
Read the critique of merely conventional subjects in its source setting.
Notice a specific revision to a refrain.
Direct praise toward the Blessed Beauty and describe servitude carefully.
shortened: During the sacred festivals and other occasions, compose brilliant odes in praise of the Blessed Beauty, and if you wish to mention 'Abdu'l-Baha, at the end of the ode or lyric simply make a mention of the servitude and effacement of this evanescent servant and implore the Divine Threshold in utter humility that he may be assisted to serve and enabled to be faithful at the Sacred Threshold.

order.why: Receive an ode valued for its meaning of servitude.
shortened: Your ode of servitude arrived and perfect joy and delight was obtained from its sweet contents and delightful meanings, for it spoke of the servitude of this evanescent atom at the Sacred Threshold of the Most Great Name.

order.why: Observe the deliberate adaptation of a quoted line to a chosen name.
shortened: "I am deaf when called by my name, yet truly, when addressed as 'Abdu'l-Baha, I hear." This verse is from previous poets and its second line is: "When addressed as 'O His servant,' I hear." But I became so enamored with the theme of this verse that I changed "O His servant" to "'Abdu'l-Baha."

order.why: Keep the separately quoted earlier form beside that adaptation.
shortened: The Arab poet saith:
"Deaf am I when called in the tribe by my name,
Yet when addressed as His servant, how keen is my ear!"

order.why: Read the naming of Abdu’l-Baha and truth in another poetic address.
shortened: "Whence comes this minstrel who hath spoken my name?
'Abdu'l-Baha is my name, truth my aim!"

order.why: Notice which verse brings particular delight and why.
Recognize the joy of reciting eloquent poems.
Read an ode through the imagery of pearls and stars.
shortened: Thy marvelous ode, which in its eloquence and fluency was like hidden and treasured pearls and stars, was read with the utmost joy and delight and recited with abundant gladness.

order.why: Let flowing water describe a festival poem.
shortened: O you who are enkindled with the fire of love! The brilliant ode and luminous unique verse that, like flowing water, streamed and flowed from your talent in celebration of the Festival of Ridvan was like pure crystal water, sweeter than the Salsabil spring.

order.why: Connect composition and chanting with the gladness of a community.
shortened: O bird of the garden of truth! Your sweet melodies and wondrous, sugary songs bring joy to the hearts of the friends and are the cause of spiritual delight. The odes that you compose and chant in praise of the Ancient Beauty (may my spirit be sacrificed for His loved ones) bestow eternal life upon the spirit and grant happiness and gladness to the heart.

order.why: Retain the historical comparison with a poet of the Prophet.
shortened: Ka'b ibn Zuhayr composed one ode in praise of the Prophet and became renowned throughout the horizons, and this accomplished poet has composed numerous odes in praise of the Most Great Name - consider then what shall come to pass.

order.why: Keep the reported identification of a community’s poet.
Preserve the name-based wordplay in praise of poetic accomplishment.
Hear the opening announcement of rose-time.
Read spring through the rose and nightingale of truth.
Follow an extended garden of gratitude into a quoted refrain.
Set a shining Sinai and blooming landscape beside a sleeping world.
Imagine a valley becoming a garden of unity.
See separation’s night turning toward a morning of vision.
Read the newly risen Youth through garden and fire imagery.
Keep the brief refrain of glad tidings and arrival.
Read the impossibility of adequate praise through multiplying resurrections.
shortened:
Were I to describe this Manifestation's praise,
A hundred thousand trumpet blasts could not convey;

For in each instant from It a hundred resurrections spring,
And in each, the spreading of a Greater Rising doth display.

Were I to attempt describing just one Rising fair,
A hundred resurrections would pass, yet still unfinished there.

order.why: Ask the hidden candle to illuminate the horizons.
Offer the soul through the poem’s joined images of sun and Sinai.
Let the repeated call to awaken invite participation.
Join a received ode to a call for attentive hearing.
Read the candle and song as ways of rousing other voices.
Move from silence toward making love known.
shortened: O thou candle of the assemblage of the merciful friends! Upon thee be the glory of God and His grace and His generosity and His gift and His eternal light! The time has come for thee to burn away the veil of silence and muteness with the kindled divine fire and to make the beauty of the Joseph of the love of God available in the marketplace and renowned throughout all horizons.

order.why: Carry the poem’s light from East toward West.
shortened: O ye beloved friends of 'Abdu'l-Baha!
Twenty-five years ago a poem was written by the Pen of the Covenant, a portion whereof reads as follows:
In the Orient scatter perfumes, and shed splendours on the West.
Carry light unto the Bulgar, and the Slav with life invest.

order.why: Introduce the seeker with a lamp longing for a human being.
Keep the separately attributed version of that search.
Preserve another source’s form of the lamp-bearing seeker.
Read the image applied to finding a person in a particular land.
Set the scriptural trust beside the yearning for heroic humanity.
shortened: "Lo! We offered the trust unto the heavens and the earth and the hills, but they shrank from bearing it and were afraid of it. And man assumed it."
"My heart is wearied by these weak-natured people - I long for the Lion of God and Rustam, son of Zal!"

order.why: Hear that yearning amid an inability to describe sorrow.
shortened: O thou who hast clung to the hem of grandeur! From the intensity of sorrows and pain, the pen hath no power to write, nor the tongue strength to speak. Of these weak-natured people my heart is weary - I long for the Lion of God and Rustam, the hero of legend!

order.why: Recognize the rose and sun beyond their place of appearance.
shortened: They conduct themselves according to these verses of Rumi:
"The branch of the rose, wherever it may grow, is still a rose
The vessel of wine, wherever it may ferment, is still wine
If the sun should rise from the West
It is still the sun itself, not something else."

order.why: Consider the relation between visible beauty and an upper reality.
Enter the cluster of verses on love’s distance, inadequate speech and the Friend’s name.
shortened:
"'Attar traversed love's seven cities,
While we remain in the bend of a single lane.

"Were people not veiled and dense,
And were throats not constricted and weak,
In thy praise I would render justice to meaning,
And would open lips with speech other than this."
When I heard mention of the Friend, I immediately arose and said:

"Whence comes this musician who spoke the Friend's name?
That I might sacrifice my soul and garment for the Friend's message.
The heart comes alive with hope for the beloved's faithfulness,
The soul dances to the melody of the Friend's words."

order.why: Listen to the paradox of an ear beyond ordinary hearing.
Keep Sa’di’s brief question about the musician.
Read the fuller quoted response to hearing the Friend named.
Retain the short form addressed through a name.
Keep the separate wording of the minstrel couplet.
Read the instruction to sing the verses of love’s bewilderment.
Preserve the same stanza in its independent source.
Retain the further separately sourced stanza without merging it.
Meet the Friend’s dawn arrival and awakened heart.
Explore the tress and grain as a snare for the heart-bird.
shortened: The tresses of the Beloved are a snare, the dark mole is the grain;
Each strand hath caught the heart-bird fast---no rest for one insane.

order.why: Read fragrance and entanglement through an address to the Beloved.
shortened: O my Lord! This loop of Baha fell into that collar of tribulation which was Thy hair. Every fragrance of musk that reaches the senses arises from Thy sweet nature.

order.why: Consider the image of standing outside the ring of a tress.
shortened: Until the ring of His tress becomes the collar of someone's neck - Oh we who stand proud outside the circle!

order.why: Read the city’s commotion through the Beloved’s features.
shortened: There is no commotion in the city except the curl of the Beloved's tress; There is no tumult in the horizons except the arch of the Friend's brow.

order.why: Keep the Sa’di attribution and its particular wording.
Retain the distinct source’s version of that image.
Hear the same image as a promise of what will be observed.
shortened: Soon thou shalt observe that:
"There is no tumult in the city save from the curling locks of the Beloved,
No commotion in the world save from the arched eyebrow of the Friend."

order.why: Keep the compressed image of longing that permits no easy rest.
shortened: No heart yearns toward that Beloved with desire, No one sleeps with such a rose-cheeked one in their garment.

order.why: Read the inherited gendered imagery within its historical poetic setting.
shortened: How excellent is what was said:
No heart yearns for any beloved save that One
None can sleep peacefully with such a Rose-cheeked One in their garment
Either go like women and choose color and fragrance
Or enter like men and cast your ball in the field

Now praise be to God that the friends of God in all regions stand firm in the Cause of God and steadfast in the love of God - they are heroes of the field and are set ablaze with the fire of the love of God.

order.why: Preserve the culturally particular descriptive lines attributed to Rumi.
shortened: O thou who speaketh in remembrance of God!

Rumi, in his Ghazals and in the Mathnavi, relateth this tale: "He saith unto thee in thy state of intoxication: O Abu'l-Hasan! O thou young in years! O thou of tender frame! O thou but lately weaned from milk! With face of a Hashimite, nape of a Turk, hair of a Daylamite, and beard of a Greek!"

order.why: Keep the playful quoted imagery and matchmaking setting identifiable.
Read a remembered performance and the smile it receives.
Attend to the alternating laughter, tears, speech and listening of an encounter.
shortened: When the taper of Tiraz lit up his countenance in the gathering of mystery, with a face full of glad-tidings and visage of joy, in the utmost grace and beauty did he meet with me, and with perfect sweetness did he begin to speak. He wept and laughed, spoke and listened, until the meeting drew to a close. At times he bloomed like a flower, and at times like a wine-vessel he was full of tumult and commotion.

order.why: Imagine the desired dance through cup and tress.
Retain the separate application of that dancing couplet.
Notice the playful reversal of a familiar claim about catching the Phoenix.
Let multiple quoted motifs enter a shared musical gathering.
shortened: Take in hand the overflowing cup of the love of God and dance in this gathering, crying out and playing this melody:
"In one hand the wine-cup, in the other the Beloved's tress
In such a dance midst this arena is my heart's desire
Weary am I of these weak-natured folk
The Lion of God and Rustam the Hero is my heart's desire"

Take up the harp and lute and raise a melody in harmony with the Supreme Concourse, that the birds of the meadow may come into rapture and ecstasy, and all may become engaged in one voice in praising and glorifying the Glorious Lord.

order.why: Preserve the passage from poetic intoxication to a practical matter of receipts.
shortened: So raise up a cry and say:
"I am intoxicated with the wine of love, drunk and inebriated with wine;
O musician play a melody, O cupbearer give me the cup!"
Regarding the receipts you had written about - we presented that amount to you.

order.why: Keep another formulation of the invitation to musician and cupbearer.
shortened: "I know not this or that, I am intoxicated with the cup of love
O musician play a melody, O cupbearer pass round the chalice!"
And upon you be greetings and praise.

order.why: Distinguish spiritual wine from the literal drink rejected in the surrounding counsel.
shortened: The fever of love cannot be broken by what is in the tavern
O Cupbearer, bring an ocean of that spiritual wine!
Counsel all souls that when the everlasting cup and divine wine are available, no pure nature would be attracted to this transient, putrid water.

order.why: Read the wine-seller as an unexpected keeper of a mystery.
Keep the Hafiz attribution to harp and lute speaking in secret.
shortened: Hafiz of Shiraz has said: "Do you know what the harp and lute are saying? Drink wine in secret, for they pronounce accusations of infidelity."

order.why: Retain the separate form of the same quoted counsel.
shortened: As the poet says: "Knowest thou what the harp and lute are saying? Drink wine in secret, for they accuse of infidelity."

order.why: Read another use of the verse within a particular instruction.
shortened: In the words of Ḥafiz of Shiraz, the purport of this verse must be followed:
"Do you know what the harp and lute are saying?
Drink wine in secret, for they pronounce it forbidden."

order.why: Keep the Hafiz citation joining the crescent, cup and hope for peace.
Preserve the compressed image of a pure draught.
Keep the explicit Ibn al-Farid attribution and its wording.
Place the quoted draught within a call to compose odes.
Read the fountain of love through the language of ritual departure.
shortened: In the words of Hafiz of Shiraz: "The moment I performed my ablutions at the fountain of love, I said four takbirs over all that exists."

order.why: Consider release from descriptions as part of a poetic journey.
Ask what could obstruct the relation between lover and beloved.
Set companionship with Joseph above monetary exchange.
Hear the remembered childhood line about sufficiency in the Beloved.
shortened: In childhood this verse was heard: "When I have Thee I have all; naught else do I need."

order.why: Locate contentment in companionship even in a well.
Keep the recorded prayer for friendship and protection.
Read shared intimacy and unity through Rumi’s contrasting souls.
shortened: How excellent is what was said:

"Indeed I have been alone with the Beloved, and between us
Was a secret more subtle than the breeze when it stirs"
The spirits of these companions are united and their breaths intermingled, even as Rumi, the mystic, says:

"The souls of wolves and dogs are separate indeed
But united are the souls of the lions of God"
For they drink from one cup and are sustained from one chalice, they sit upon one carpet and dwell in one station.

order.why: Preserve the separate citation of the souls-of-lions image.
shortened: As Rumi says: The souls of wolves and dogs are separate from one another, but united are the souls of the lions of God.

order.why: Let the reported longing distinguish a place from its people.
shortened: Heart yearns for the abode of peace,
Where the builder of wall resides.
But my longing is not for the city,
Nay, it is for the dwellers of the city.

order.why: Keep the reported Hafiz citation and its geographical imagery.
shortened: "That is the river, and this is the bank thereof, of which the poet Hafiz has thus written: 'O zephyr, shouldst thou pass by the banks of the Araxes, implant a kiss on the earth of that valley and make fragrant thy breath. Hail, a thousand times hail, to thee, O abode of Salma! How dear is the voice of thy camel-drivers, how sweet the jingling of thy bells!'

order.why: Imagine the disruption caused by departure and arrival.
shortened:
A moon went forth from this city -- toward another it fled;
By its setting and its rising, two cities turned o'erhead.

order.why: Remember companionship before hearing the ache of separation.
shortened: O longtime friend! Remember those days when in Iraq we reclined in the shade of the Tree of Providence, and in every hour through increased favors and bounties we reached the utmost of our desires. Remember those bright nights and those times like rose gardens and flower beds that passed. How well did the poet say:
Come, rosebud-mouthed beloved, see how straitened is this heart in me;
Yet still I breathe, bereft of thee---Behold my hard heart’s cruelty.

order.why: Read a letter’s sweetness through constancy and listening.
shortened: O cherished and honored friend,

The purport of thy letter was exceedingly sweet, for it betokened faithfulness and expressed steadfastness and constancy in love, inasmuch as thou hast not forgotten me, and with attentive ears desirest to hear the melody of divine inspiration.

order.why: Hope to mend separation’s torn garment.
shortened: If we remain alive we shall mend
The garment that separation has rent
The rest is prayer for your happiness.

order.why: Keep the separate short formulation of that hope.
shortened: If we remain alive we will mend the garment that has been torn by separation.

order.why: Seek a lost rose’s fragrance in rosewater.
Retain the independent Mathnavi citation and source omission.
Hear the poet’s comparison of death and separation.
shortened: I testify that the Arab poet said: "They say that death is difficult for youth, but by God, separation from loved ones is more difficult."

order.why: Preserve the heightened language of weeping and burning.
Read festival joy and private sorrow together.
shortened: They are in celebration and excitement, in joy and delight, while this servant, with weeping eyes and a burning heart, recites this verse:
"It is the season of festival, yet we are hopeless of seeing the Beloved
The world is in feasting and drinking, while we have tear-filled eyes"
However, this weeping is the source of laughter, and this grief and sorrow is the pride of all joys.

order.why: Keep the further festival lament and hope for renewed fellowship.
Enter the long prose-poetic landscape of grief and separation.
Retain the reported lament naming places of suffering.
shortened: Nayriz burneth with fever, and my sorrow-filled heart sheddeth blood,
How consumed my soul is, of what Adharbayjan hath wrought.

order.why: Set poetic language beside an account of women’s actual persecution.
Read the concrete account of widespread upheaval and dispossession.
shortened: O friends of 'Abdu'l-Baha! Although the upheaval in Iran is severe and trials and tribulations have overcome everyone near and far, all parties are impatient and restless, each group is overwhelmed with grief and sorrow, blood has been spilled and homes have fallen, property has been plundered and pillaged, and leaders have become homeless, many leaders have crept into corners of oblivion and all the tribes and peoples of Iran have become scattered and dispersed. Inevitably in this tumult and commotion the friends too must experience some difficulty.

order.why: Keep the quoted hope attached to a photograph of a prisoner in chains.
Hear the elegy’s repeated personal address.
Read a prison chain transformed through Joseph imagery.
shortened:
The chain that bound the Joseph of the prison turns to mercy's chain,
And Egypt, in the realm of truth, o'er every land is king again.

order.why: Preserve the Turkish quotation and its repeated Persian rendering.
Compare the Persian, Turkish and Arabic images of vulnerability.
Keep the brief image of tumult in every atom.
Recognize the winds that do not follow human wishes.
Read the house and flood as images of accepting trial.
shortened: As the poet has said:
We who have given heart and sight to the flood of tribulation,
Let the torrent of grief come and tear the house from its foundation!

order.why: Preserve the drowning metaphor and visible source omission.
Consider the elephant-keeper’s house as a figure for accepting a demanding commitment.
shortened: As the poet says:
"Either make not friendship with elephant-keepers
Or build a house worthy of an elephant
Or like men enter the field and toss the ball
Make your breast the target of every affliction and your heart the aim of every cruelty."

order.why: Read the quoted examples of Abraham, John, Joseph and Jesus with their application to a person’s sufferings.
Keep the distinct use of that sequence to encourage endurance.
shortened: The Persian poet said:
If like Abraham one must enter the fire
Or like John have my blood flow free
Or like Joseph be cast in well and prison
Or through poverty become like Jesus son of Mary

Now consider that if souls who in past ages became so intoxicated with just a whiff of the fragrances of the love of God that they accepted the cup of trials, how much more should we who are bewildered by the cup of bounty in this Day of Manifestation remain alive and fresh despite severe tribulations.

order.why: Preserve the extravagant language of sacrifice alongside its hope for comfort.
shortened: How well was it said:
"A hundred thousand living hearts are needed on this path
To sacrifice a hundred lives with every breath"
Despite this, there is hope that the means of ancient comfort will be provided through His aid, grace and bounty.

order.why: Read the paradoxical life-and-death lines in their devotional address.
shortened: Surely he must have said "My soul be sacrificed for You" a hundred thousand times and recited: "Die if you would be a devoted lover, for you have done all else yet still live," and cried out with his heart's tongue: "Kill me, kill me, O trustworthy ones, for in my death is life upon life."

order.why: Keep the severe personification of love within the quoted poem.
Preserve the demanding poetic speech without converting it into literal advice.
Read poison and wounds as the poem’s paradoxical vocabulary of longing.
shortened: What is the medicine of the yearning one? Poison from the hand of the Beloved.
What is the balm of the lovers? Wounds from the arm of the Friend.

order.why: Keep the separately cited version and its closing greeting.
Retain the quotation that describes love’s ease as suffering.
shortened: How excellent is what was said: "Live detached, for love's comfort is suffering - its beginning is illness and its end is death."

order.why: Introduce the fuller cup of trial as a familiar poetic image.
shortened: As the skilled poet has said:
"Whoever in this feast is more favored is given a fuller cup of tribulation."

order.why: Keep the distinct wording about nearness and the cup of woe.
Read the image as a wish to share another’s trial.
shortened: How excellent are the words of the poet:
"Whoever in this feast is more favored
Is given a fuller cup of trial"
God willing, 'Abdu'l-Baha too shall have a share of this supreme gift and receive a portion, that He may become thy partner and companion in this.

order.why: Set pearl and arrow beside hope that hardship leads to rest.
Retain the quotation’s presence alongside an unrelated practical answer about the Hands.
Read the pearl-and-arrow lines offered to encourage patience.
Notice the explicit wish for the pearl of bounty rather than calamity for the addressee.
shortened: Although in the blessed Tablets this verse of Sana'i is written: "If He bestows the pearl of bounty, behold the hearts are its shells, and if the arrow of calamity comes, behold the souls are its targets," yet for you I wish the pearl of bounty, not the arrow of calamity.

order.why: Keep the brief poetic expression about bitter words and sweet lips.
shortened: As the poet says: "Bitter words befit those sugar-dispensing ruby lips."

order.why: Let the bitter-to-sweet image become a counsel of patience.
Read the hope that bitter days will pass.
shortened: How excellent is what was said:
"These bitter days, more bitter than poison, shall pass
Once again days sweet as sugar shall come."

order.why: Quotes poetry of consolation amid turmoil.
Hear the Turkish and Persian expressions of transience together.
Preserve the separately attributed Hafiz line and its source omission.
shortened: Hafiz has said:
"These bitter days, more bitter than poison, shall pass; Once again days sweet as sugar shall come."...

order.why: Apply the remembered lines to named people who are troubled.
Receive consolation through Joseph’s anticipated return.
shortened: O servant of the Abha Beauty! Hafiz of Shiraz says:
"The lost Joseph shall return to Canaan, grieve not,
The house of sorrows shall one day become a rose garden, grieve not."

order.why: Read the quoted ghazal within an address to someone bereaved.
shortened: O Aqa Darvish! The Beauty of the All-Glorious - may my spirit and essence be sacrificed for His loved ones - says at the end of a famous ghazal:
O dervish, the world has burned from this soul-consuming flame
Divine One! It is time to revive it through this plaintive cry
After the passing of your child and the death of your dear one, do not be sorrowful and grief-stricken.

order.why: Hear the related cry to revive through a plaintive song.
Consider a hidden seed as the beginning of a garden.
Read life from death and rose from thorn as images of renewal.
Retain the poetic hope in renewed assistance of the Holy Spirit.
shortened: Let us see what the power of the Friend's arm can do - If the Holy Spirit's grace should help again, Others too will do what Jesus did.

order.why: Keep the reported scriptural sequence of seasons and times.
Read the example of many unanswered letters without complaint.
Preserve the sharp poetic reply to criticism beside the counsel not to increase clamor.
shortened: The Arab poet said:
"When criticism comes to you from one who is deficient
It is testimony that I am perfect"
In any case, you should not mention anything further in Chihrihnama that would cause an increase in anyone's clamor.

order.why: Keep the reported couplet about a reversal in conduct.
Distinguish an imitated cry from the message it should carry.
Read the instruction to sing a related warning about imitation.
Keep the concise question about the hoopoe’s secret.
shortened: Though the sand grouse may learn the call of the hoopoe, where is the hoopoe's secret and the message from Saba?

order.why: Ask what service has actually been offered.
shortened: How well did the poet say:
"How can I raise my head before the Friend in shame,
When no worthy service has come from my hand?"

order.why: Retain the parallel question in its own source.
shortened: How excellent are these words:
How can I raise my head before the Friend in shame,
For no worthy service came forth from my hand?

order.why: Let a passing year prompt reflection on pleasing the Beloved.
shortened:
How excellent was that which was said, and how excellent was he who said it:
The year hath passed, and would that I knew
Whether anyone hath achieved that which pleaseth Thee.

order.why: Read the fire of love with the explanation of servitude.
shortened: Kindle the fire of love and burn away all existence,
Then take a step and enter the path of the lovers
The praise of this servant in the world of creation is worship at the Sacred Threshold and servitude at the Threshold of the Divine Unity.

order.why: Keep the separately quoted call to enter the lovers’ path.
Preserve the remembered line from the famous poem.
shortened: The Most Glorious Beauty - may my spirit be sacrificed for His loved ones - says in the famous poem: "This is the way and custom, if you seek union with Baha - seek it!"

order.why: Read the fuller challenging invitation to the path within its song.
Read watchfulness at the Door as sovereignty of heart and soul.
shortened:
Whoever keeps watch at that exalted Door
Becomes the warden of a realm secure;

The kingdom of the soul, the heart's domain,
Finds in his hand a sovereign's reign.

order.why: Contrast earthly kingship and poverty through sacred imagery.
Retain the particular incident and the poetic response to dispossession.
Keep the recollected Sana’i poem and its instruction about idols.
Let the poem’s paired questions remain open.
shortened: Is the bottom of the sea better or the surface?
Is His arrow more alluring or the shield?

order.why: Imagine restoring sight through Joseph’s garment.
shortened: Like the Egyptian herald bearing Joseph's garment, you may open the eyes of the Jacobs and perfume their nostrils with the fragrance of Joseph's spiritual garment.

order.why: Turn the tailor’s imagery toward mending wounds and covering faults.
Make generosity and forgiveness the poem’s petition.
Ask for a drop of knowledge to be joined to the sea.
Pray for people to become sources of light and life.
shortened: I beseech God that they may become the light of hearts and bestow self-sacrifice upon souls, that they may become like laughing hundred-petaled roses in the heavenly garden and flowing cypresses by the stream of knowledge.

order.why: Preserve the practical counsel on steadfastness, wisdom and kindness.
shortened: If it were not so, such success would not have been achieved, for success is paired with steadfastness, and every precious steadfast soul is promised the confirmation of the Gracious Lord. "Those who say 'Our Lord is God' and then remain steadfast - the angels descend upon them." Therefore, if Haji deems it advisable, you may return to Burujin with utmost dignity but with perfect wisdom, forbearance and good conduct. Inspire and encourage the divine friends with the fragrances of the All-Merciful, spiritual attractions and merciful sentiments, so that all may associate and conduct themselves with utmost kindness toward all people.

order.why: Keep the sustained prose encouragement and its account of trial.
shortened: One must look to the end result, and the end belongs to the righteous. The gloating of enemies and reproach of the unfaithful are like medicine for the sick - though bitter at first, it becomes sweet in the end. Whatever befalls one in the path of the love of God is a blessing.

order.why: Retain the Firdawsi citation’s play upon the addressee’s name.
Keep the Rumi citation’s numerical image of inclusion.
Read personified Generosity in the praise of a family.
Preserve the Ferdowsi comparison of bodily power and spiritual character.
Hear the reported appeal to a morning breeze as messenger.
Keep the reported translated verse with its own rhetorical question.
Include the remembered street song’s ordinary playfulness.
Retain the reported Gospel allusion among the original selections.
Keep the brief invocation exactly as the source supplies it.
shortened: In the Name of the All-Powerful, the Almighty!

order.why: Ask for a song that gladdens one who feels deprived.
shortened: So in this rose garden, like a nightingale with wondrous melodies, raise for this captive of deprivation a song and tune of servitude at the Threshold, that my heart and soul may be gladdened and my conscience and consciousness may be fulfilled.

order.why: Close among diverse flowers and birds, each expressing the life of the garden.
shortened: One, like a rose, has rent their garment, while another, like a nightingale, has sent their lament to the heavens. One, like the narcissus with languid eyes, has opened eyes of wonder, while another, like a meadow violet, has fallen intoxicated in the wilderness and plain. One, like the cypress, has raised their stature tall, while another, like the ringdove, has caused commotion in the rose garden.

questions: Which image or repeated line most changes your perception when you read it aloud, and how does it do so?
How does a quoted verse gain a new meaning from the letter, encounter, or counsel in which it appears?
What helps distinguish poetic images of wine, wounds, or surrender from literal instructions?
How do the readings connect the craft of composition with sincerity, meaning, and service?
What different forms of consolation emerge from the poems of separation, patience, grief, and reunion?
How might poetry deepen attention to another person’s experience while leaving room for meanings we cannot fully explain?

references.label: 1 · Song of Songs 2:10–14 · Springtime and the beloved voice
references.note: Read the invitation to rise and come away as winter passes, flowers appear, and birds are heard. Attend also to the desire to hear the beloved’s voice. Compare these images with the compilation’s roses, nightingales, and moments when a name brings joy. What can shared imagery disclose while each poem retains its own voice and setting?

subjects.displayTitle: Learning from history: memory, power, and the fruits of a life
subjects.introduction: Bahá’u’lláh teaches that the future can be read in the mirror of the past, and the first thing that mirror shows is ourselves: people who condemn the tyrants of yesterday while repeating their deeds, as though exempt from the grave. Looking back honestly is thus a spiritual discipline. It asks where Alexander and the Caesars have gone, whose skulls in the dust cannot be told from their subjects’, and finds in the battles of nations a succession of waves that rise on one another and vanish. Yet the same gaze uncovers what endures: the trustworthiness of a thief who would not betray a king’s salt, apostles whose obscure deaths outlasted empires, cities that flourished through learning and withered through heedlessness. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says the purpose of history is to awaken those who come after, which makes memory a responsibility, the discipline Deuteronomy urges on a people comfortable enough to forget who delivered them [1]. The inquiry runs on into the past and future of Iran, the early history of Islam, and the cycles by which civilizations rise and decline.
subjects.arc: Begin with self-examination and truthful historical inquiry; confront impermanence and the cost of conquest; explore civilization, religious renewal and remembered events; close with enduring service and history as an invitation to action.

order.why: Open with the past as a mirror of the future.
shortened: Say: O ye that have eyes to see! The past is the mirror of the future. Gaze ye therein and be apprised thereof; perchance ye may be aided thereby to recognize the Friend and may be not the cause of His displeasure.

order.why: Immediately turn criticism of past tyranny back upon present conduct.
shortened: Today people deny the deeds of those who tyrannized in the past, while they commit tyranny worse than what was committed before, and they perceive it not. It is as though they feel secure from the grave and are guaranteed immortality.

order.why: Make truthful history an explicit aim of inquiry.
Question repeated tales that lack clear evidence.
Allow time for the meaning of events to emerge.
Measure conquest against suffering and wasted human labor.
Read admiration for a monument alongside remembrance of its human cost.
shortened: Calling 'Abdul Baha's attention to the monument, I remarked that it was higher than the Great Pyramid, whereupon 'Abdul Baha said that to many people the great Pyramid was the most to be admired structure in Egypt, but to him it had always produced an unpleasing impression, for it recalled to his mind the intense suffering of the thousands of slaves and captives who were under the oppressor who built the pyramid for his tomb.

order.why: Ask what practical learning from other societies can offer.
shortened: Those who maintain that these modern concepts apply only to other countries and are irrelevant in Iran, that they do not satisfy her requirements or suit her way of life, disregard the fact that other nations were once as we are now. Did not these new systems and procedures, these progressive enterprises, contribute to the advancement of those countries? Were the people of Europe harmed by the adoption of such measures? Or did they rather by these means reach the highest degree of material development?

order.why: Invite close attention to varied people, circumstances and events.
shortened: Look with penetrating vision into the earlier centuries - their conditions, their traces, their phases, their distinguished ones, and the wondrous events that transpired therein, their mysterious secrets, the diverse dispositions of their men, and the varying tastes of their luminaries - for verily the accounts of those who have gone before are a reminder and lesson to those who follow.

order.why: Name reflection on predecessors as a way to gain insight.
shortened: In the former generations that have passed away, there are lessons for us. When we consider our predecessors, their ways, and their worldly success and prosperity, we gain insight.

order.why: Consider the reported account of history as an awakening of later generations.
shortened: The purpose of history is to awaken those who come after. See in what path those who came before achieved success and prosperity, and follow that same path.
How wonderful it would have been if the history of the Prophets had been properly written, for it would then have served as a model for this time.

order.why: Join reflection on scripture with attention to bygone ages.
shortened: Say: Ponder ye on that which He hath sent down unto you, then observe and reflect upon the bygone ages and what God hath decreed therein.

order.why: Seek to avoid repeating earlier failures.
Ask what fruit past deeds actually produced.
shortened: Say: O ye who have gone astray! What was the outcome of all that the former people said and did, and what fruit did they reap?

order.why: Consider the relation of recurring patterns to hope for better times.
shortened: Consider the past and the events that transpired therein. Is not the future like unto the past? Is not the past the very mirror of the future? Truly, that which thou findest in the past thou wilt see in the future, for both are subject to the same order. But each and all complain of the past and look expectantly toward the future, hopeful that their times of toil and weariness might pass, and that days of joy and peace may soon arrive.

order.why: Keep the claims about early historiography and scripture in their source setting.
shortened: The histories prior to Alexander, which were based on oral accounts current among the people, were put together later on. There are great discrepancies among them, and certainly they can never hold their own against Holy Writ. It is an accepted fact among historians themselves that these histories were compiled after Alexander, and that prior to his time history was transmitted by word of mouth.

order.why: Read the reported distinction between oral transmission and witnessed events.
shortened: In former cycles people used to relate by tradition the things which happened during the time of the Prophets; for instance, the disciples explained the miracles during the time of Christ; these statements were oral. But in this great day facts are established; what Baha'u'llah has performed was seen by the eyes.

order.why: Retain the historical account of writing and its period vocabulary.
Consider how new events can displace collective memory.
shortened: One that occurred a thousand years ago is forgotten in one that is taking place today. Some events occur which take away the memory of all past incidents. The incidents which occurred previous to the coming of Adam have vanished, because those which have occurred since have entirely erased them from the mind of man.

order.why: Read the reported archaeological example of Nineveh.
Keep the separately reported Nineveh and Jonah account identifiable.
Explore the reported distinction between a legend and the truth it can convey.
Retain the proposed interpretation of ancient lifespans and calendars.
shortened: O servant of the Abha Beauty! Regarding the mention of the length of life of the ancients, this is a relative matter, not according to current convention in these days. For in ancient times there were different kinds of years - some would count one lunar cycle as a year, some would count the solar cycle, and likewise they would name the cycle of each planet as a year, such as the lunar year, solar year, Venus year, Mercury year, Mars year, Jupiter year, and Saturn year, which refers to the orbital period of these planets.

order.why: Enter the extended interrogation of vanished sovereign power.
shortened: Reflect upon the generations of old. Where is Alexander and his like? Where are their victorious standards and their upraised banners? Where are their brandished spears and their flying arrows? Where are their outstretched necks and their lofty palaces?

God hath brought them down from the highest chambers of their palaces to the lowest depths of their graves. Were anyone to search therein, could he distinguish the skulls of kings from subjects, or the fingers of the wealthy from the destitute?

order.why: Hear Alexander’s silence interpreted in the reported conversation.
Read vanished waves and the ruined royal dwelling together.
shortened: Whoso ponders the lessons of history will learn that this sea has lifted up innumerable waves, yet in the end each has dissolved and vanished, like a shadow drifting by. The waves have perished, but the sea lives on.

Gracious God! That royal edifice was once splendidly decked forth and fair. But there are spiders' webs today, where hung the curtains of gold brocade, and where the king's drums beat and his musicians played, the only sound is the harsh cries of kites and crows. "This is verily the capital of the owl's realm, where thou wilt hear no sound, save only the echo of his repeated calls."

order.why: Extend the wave image through a sequence of conquests.
shortened: Where is that Persian wave, where is that Alexandrian wave, where is that wave of Roman Augustus, where is that Arab wave, where is that wave of Bonaparte, where is that wave of Charlemagne, where is that wave of Hannibal - all vanished, dominion does not endure.
Physical conquests have no permanence; it is divine conquests that endure.

order.why: Observe rise and decline through human, plant and dynastic life.
Let the ruined palace become both warning and consolation.
shortened: Where is the splendor of Parviz and his golden hoard, where is the leisure of the powerful and their tall mansions, where is the wealth of the tyrants and their serried hosts? Wert thou to see the palace of Khosrow today, thou wouldst find it barren save for the reverberations of the echo and the spider's web.
Profit by their example, O thou endued with understanding, and grieve not over that which hath befallen thee.

order.why: Keep the separate description of Ctesiphon and its quoted echo.
Turn the graves of rulers into a summons to reflection.
Remember that greater power did not confer permanence.
shortened: Say: O people! Consider the generations of the past and what befell them, though they were mightier than you in strength, greater than you in glory, and more exalted than you in station. All of them went to their places and were buried with their deeds and returned to dust as they began the first time - and this is the evident truth.

order.why: Place remembrance of vanished treasure beside reliance upon God.
Retain the scriptural and historical catalogue of fallen peoples.
shortened: By God! Verily in the peoples of Noah, Hud, Lot, and Thamud, and the dwellers of Al-Hijr, and the Jews, and the kings of Saba, and the tyrants of Mecca, and the Caesars of the spacious lands, and the Chosroes of the crooked city, and the overthrown cities of ancient times, there is indeed a lesson for those possessed of understanding and insight who can discern the ends of things from their beginnings.

order.why: Consider the contrast between earthly life and enduring fruit.
shortened: Look at the kings and queens who have passed! They all lie under the earth. No name and no trace, nor any monument or surviving fruit remained of them. Their life belonged to the world of dust and consequently it passed away and was extinguished.

order.why: Read the loss of royal families beside the promised endurance of faithful service.
shortened: In this century, how many families of kings and princes who were at the height of glory and wealth were scattered, left destitute and perished. But praise be to God that the loved ones of God day by day had their foundation made lofty and their structure made firm. They are successful in both worlds and eternal glory is specially theirs, even in the center of this dust-heap.

order.why: Walk through the reported landscape of scattered monuments.
shortened: When a traveler passes through one of those old Saharas he sees here a monolith. "What is this?" he inquires "This is the last remain of the once flourishing Greek culture." the guide answers him. Then he observes dilapidated temples, tall granite pillars, miles of aqueducts, half-buried palaces, ivy-covered amphitheatres, excavated mausoleums. "What are these?" he asks with incredible amazement. "Oh! these are the silent tales of mighty civilizations."

order.why: Let travel broaden the perspective of the observer.
shortened: Travelling is a very good thing. It opens the eyes and broadens the horizon. In the East one may behold vast and desert places where one lay peopled towns; this shows the Hand of Almighty God.

When travelling one makes discoveries of strange things--i.e. The Emperors of Rome ruled over many thousands of people and were famous and powerful, but now the Emperors are dead and their power has vanished.

order.why: Preserve the reported words about buried cities with their attribution.
Distinguish transient achievement from the enduring Cause of the Kingdom.
shortened: In this mortal world every important matter hath an end; and every remarkable achievement a termination; none having permanent existence. For instance, consider how the important achievements of the ancient world have been totally exterminated and not a trace remaineth therefrom save the great Cause of the Kingdom of God, which hath no beginning and will have no end.

order.why: Read national pride in celebrated rulers through the image of setting stars.
shortened: Today the people of the West take the utmost pride in Napoleon I, that such a great personage appeared in France. Germany glories in Frederick the Great, that such a renowned figure arose in Germany. Russia takes pride in Peter the Great, that such a dragon became a champion in the realm of Russia. England in Henry, America in Washington, and Italy in Garibaldi--in brief, every nation takes pride and glory in some renowned figure. However, all these great souls were setting stars, and "soon no trace of them, not even a whisper, will remain."

order.why: Compare the remembered lives of believers and dynasties.
shortened: Consider those souls who lived in the days of the Manifestations of God - because they believed in those holy Manifestations, their descendants take pride in them to this day.

This became a lesson - that the kings of the world who were conquerors of countries and wore crowns of emperors, like the Kayanids, Pishdadids, Sassanids, Abbasids, Umayyads and even Safavids, their lineage ended in utter abasement and lowliness.

order.why: Keep the reported contrast between Pharaoh and Moses.
shortened: Consider how lofty is His sovereignty!

Conversely, consider the case of Pharaoh. There is no sign of him, no name of him, no trace of him. The little name that remains of him is because he was a contemporary of His Holiness Moses. Otherwise, pharaohs were many.

order.why: Set forgotten rulers beside remembered service.
shortened: The traces of Kings and queens have passed away but the services of the servants of God have been handled down from century to century. The descendents of Abbas established their seat of government in Bagdad and they ruled the Islamic world for 500 yrs. Persia and Turkestan, Egypte and Arabia and as far as the confines of Indus bowed to their authority. Thirty six Khalifs appeared one after another but today their memory is forgotten.

order.why: Read Rustam’s story as a reflection on bodily prowess.
shortened: O thou Tahamtan! The legendary Rustam of Zabul, though he was a most mighty hero in the arena of bravery and courage and though in physical prowess was superior to every champion and in this wise his name was renowned in all the world, yet at the end through a ruse carried out by his brother, became entrapped in a deep pit and no trace of him didst remain.

order.why: Preserve the critical address to a namesake of Faridun.
Place beside it a different Faridun address emphasizing justice and care.
shortened: O Feridun! Thy namesake did uproot the foundations of tyranny, and cleansed the realm of foes; he raised aloft the standard of Kavian, and laid the groundwork of justice. He nurtured the priests and exalted the peasants; he was a refuge to the helpless and a loving, compassionate friend to the distressed. Do thou likewise, according to thine own measure, follow the path of the righteous ones of old.

order.why: Ask what lasting benefit follows political reconsolidation.
Keep the interrupted account of Nadir and its poetic reflection intact.
shortened: O servant of the Threshold of Baha! Your illustrious ancestor Nadir was unique in his time and a genius of that land and realm....

...that foundation ultimately collapsed and that victory became utter defeat. Palaces were transformed into tombs, and the royal diadem ended in a crypt full of fear and dread. How excellent are these words: "It is as though no one had ever dwelt between Hajun and Safa, nor had any nightly conversation taken place in Mecca. Yes, those people were there, but they were destroyed by the vicissitudes of nights and ill-fated stars."

order.why: Preserve the separately reported praise of Nadir’s capacities.
shortened: Nadir Shah was one of the great rulers of Persia and during his military career he conquered India and many other countries. He was a resourceful leader as well as a noble warrior.

order.why: Retain the cautiously attributed account of the first crowned king.
shortened: O servant at the threshold of the Lord God! According to the accounts in some ancient histories, it appears that the first king who placed a crown upon his head, sat upon the throne, and adorned the diadem of kingship was Kiyumarth.

order.why: Read the reported Siyavash narrative as a distinct traditional story.
Keep the reported salt-and-trustworthiness story in its narrative setting.
Explore the contrast between flourishing Central Asian cities and later desolation.
shortened: If one were to travel through the deserts of Central Asia he would observe how many cities, once great and prosperous like Paris and London, are now demolished and razed to the ground.

Formerly that plain bore the fruit of the finest civilizations of the past. Tokens of development and refinement were apparent all around, arts and sciences were well protected and promoted, professions and industries flourished, commerce and agriculture had reached a high stage of efficiency, and the foundations of government and statesmanship were laid on a strong and solid basis. Today that vast stretch of land hath become mostly the shelter and asylum of Turkoman tribes, and an arena for the ferocious display of wild beasts.

order.why: Read the rise of learning in Turkistan and its subsequent decline.
shortened: Divine and material sciences and arts progressed to such a degree that from the school of Turkistan emerged the geniuses of the time and the learned ones of the horizons. Even in the Persian language they gained such proficiency that the poets of Turkistan became renowned in East and West.
Afterwards decline occurred and that progress was transformed into regression. Those brilliant traces were lost and that civilizational luminosity was transformed into a strange dimness.

order.why: Bring the pattern into a particular address to Hamadan.
shortened: O loved ones of the Most Merciful in Hamadan! Verily this city of yours was once a mighty capital and the seat of supreme sovereignty in ancient times, and the fame of its people spread far and wide throughout all regions, such that past nations would follow their example in all matters pertaining to worldly prosperity. Then God stripped from them the garment of glory and wealth and clothed them in the cloak of poverty and extinction, due to how the hands of self and passion had played with their hearts.

order.why: Hear Persia’s lost prosperity within a prayer.
shortened: O Thou sanctified Lord! From its earliest days, Thou didst make the soil of Persia to be musk scented and soul stirring, gem laden and knowledge bearing.

For a time, the flame of its knowledge was extinguished and the star of its greatness hidden beneath a veil. Its vernal breezes gave way to autumnal blasts, and its delightsome rose-garden was filled with tares and thorns; its wellspring of limpid waters turned brackish and stale, and its greatest and most precious souls were made homeless wanderers in distant lands; its effulgent light was dimmed and its mighty river reduced to a narrow stream.

order.why: Retain the reported contrast between former and present Persia.
shortened: There was a time when Persia was like a fragrant Bouquet perfuming all the nostrils and she was the center of the glory and honor of the world of humanity. The inhabitants of Persia from a social, industrial, political and moral standpoint were superior to the rest of mankind.
Now the conditions are changed and the same lofty standard is not kept waving aloft. Like a great giant she is prostrated on the ground while groaning with a pitiful voice.

order.why: Read the address to Parsis through its imagery of a darkened garden.
shortened: For a time, there came a decline and negligence appeared. The moon of its glory's zenith set, and the star of its wisdom and knowledge descended. The wise became foolish and the learned became ignorant. A light shone forth from a foreign land and an army arrived from a neighboring realm. The carpet of the Persians was rolled up and the joy of the Iranians came to an end. The bright day became dark in their sight and the rose garden became a thorny wilderness.

order.why: Keep the account of Zoroastrian dispersal and renewal in its setting.
shortened: O beloved friends of 'Abdu'l-Baha! For one thousand three hundred years, the star of the Zoroastrians' existence had vanished in the west of non-existence. They had completely disappeared from sight, living scattered and disorganized, captive to the oppression of tyrants, until the world-illuminating Sun of Truth rose from the horizon of Iran.

order.why: Hear Manukji’s reported account of persecution and abasement.
shortened: When Manukji came to Bagdad and stood in His spiritual Presence he related many stories concerning the humiliation of the Parsees and how in his travels from India throughout Persia he found them in the lowest degree of dispersion and abasement; how the Persian authorities persecuted and drove them from pillar to post and how these creatures like sparrows were made captives in the cruel claws of the falcon and how they were maltreated in the cities of Yazd and Kerman.

order.why: Read the description of Persepolis and hope for renewed building as reported.
shortened: If one goes to Persepolis, one can see how buildings are constructed. Yet there is no edifice that does not fall into ruin. Persepolis, with all its grandeur, was destroyed and demolished - what then of these lesser buildings?

Now the Iranians of this time have reduced their country from that glory to this poverty and abasement, and still they strive in the ruination of their land. Indeed what ignorance does! We hope that it will again become better than before. That they will build a magnificent Mashriqu'l-Adhkar in Persepolis. That Persepolis will become more prosperous than before.

order.why: Connect changing fortunes with mindfulness and wisdom.
shortened: All things are subject to change and transformation, to ascent and decline, like the human body.

What is needed is effort and striving and hope in divine confirmation, not heedlessness, pride, vanity and laxity. Since one has no encompassing knowledge of the consequences of affairs, therefore one must always take the path of mindfulness and wisdom, and learn lessons from the past for the future.

order.why: Consider the reported Naw-Ruz gatherings as occasions of beneficent reform.
shortened: In such a day in former times, Iranians held a great festival, but in this time they are distressed. In truth, some ancient kings of Iran had a paternal relationship with their subjects and were caring. Although their sovereignty was absolute, most worked in consultation with ministers. How much the Nauruz gatherings were the cause of harmony and agreement! Every gathering in this festival became the cause of some beneficent decree. Great reforms would come about.

order.why: Read the festival through charitable institutions and aid to the poor.
Keep the particular traditional Naw-Ruz account.
Preserve the separate version of the festival’s origins.
Retain the short account of Jamshid’s religion and its disappearance.
Consider the reported account of Lycurgus and the durability of reform.
Explore the social role attributed to a common language.
Trace the reported movement of civilization across regions.
Read the reported transmission of musical learning.
Consider education that joins material and religious sciences.
Notice the unexpected benefits attributed to a search and a voyage.
Keep the reported migration account and historical racial vocabulary attributed.
Read the letter on ancient contact and forgotten divine calls.
Preserve the separate reported reflection on America, Asia and worship.
Enter the account of Moses as educator and guide.
Follow the account from Abraham through Moses and nation-building.
shortened: For after a short time the teachings of Abraham were realized in the world: The Holy Land was given to His descendants; the foundations of the religion of God were established; Isaac and Jacob came into the world; Joseph became ruler in Egypt; Ishmael was blessed and illumined Mount Paran; Moses the Interlocutor appeared, beheld in the desert of Sinai the blazing fire of God in the Burning Bush, rescued the Israelites from their oppression and captivity at the hands of the Egyptians, led them to the Holy Land, and, through His teachings and His religion, which were consonant with the needs of the age, founded a mighty nation.

order.why: Keep the reported promise to Abraham in its setting.
shortened: When Abraham was exiled from His home, God spoke to Him, "Do not be sad. I will give You the choicest land in the entire world." And if there were a land better than here, God would have given it to Abraham.

order.why: Retain the questions about fulfillment and the Holy Land.
shortened: How would the lights of the Luminary of the horizons and Sun of Truth of the world of effulgence have shone upon the regions of the world, circled the dawning-places of existence, become established in the Holy Land, and how would all the future promises to Israel have been fulfilled? And how would the gathering of Abraham's children in the Promised Land according to God's promise have been made possible?

order.why: Read spiritual power through the described transformation of a people.
Preserve the reported account of Arabia and its historically charged language.
Keep the separately reported argument about religion and civilization.
Keep the reported contrast of turning toward the Kingdom and toward mortal things.
shortened: The Jews once turned to the Kingdom, but when they looked backward to mortal things, they became dispersed. Then Christ led men to the Kingdom; their signs have remained.

order.why: Read the reported sequence from Moses to Christ.
Introduce the seasons of spiritual renewal and decline.
Keep the Christian autumn image in its source.
Explore the neglected garden as an image of lost religious vitality.
Retain the reported critique of inherited customs.
shortened: Indeed, if we were to closely consider this, we would see that the older societies are completely unaware of religion and are captives of nature. No sign of divine bounties is discerned among them, nor is any heavenly fragrance inhaled from them. They are governed by certain traditions and customs and follow the ways of their forefathers.

order.why: Keep the reported comparison of aging religious communities attributed.
Read the critique of warfare in medieval Christianity.
Consider the role assigned to self-seeking leaders.
shortened: The religions of the past have fallen into decay on account of self-seeking leaders who in the course of time appropriated all the rights and powers unto themselves and looked down contemptuously upon the rest of their co-religionists as ignorant and deprived of the knowledge of God.

order.why: Preserve the concise reported criticism of religious ministers.
Read the reported explanation of hostility to religion in France.
Keep the historically situated contrast of East and West.
Retain the reported assessment of Syria and England in context.
Read the remembered contrast between a colony’s founders and descendants.
Consider the value assigned to observing conditions directly.
Keep the reported example of medical institutions and decline.
Place contemporary irreligion beside a promise of renewed gathering.
shortened: Indeed, the face of the world hath been turned toward irreligion. In all years, nay in all months, nay in all days, it hath been far from faith, certitude and knowledge, and close to conjecture and vain imaginings. For a time it shall continue thus, even as the duration thereof hath been revealed and recorded in the Book of God. But be not thou sorrowful, for the effulgences of the Sun of Truth shall assuredly absorb the superfluous moistures of nature and shall gather together the scattered letters.

order.why: Ask why earlier people denied what they were awaiting.
shortened: And now, consider and reflect a moment upon the waywardness of this people. What could have been the reason for such denial and avoidance on their part?

Meditate profoundly, that the secret of things unseen may be revealed unto you, that you may inhale the sweetness of a spiritual and imperishable fragrance, and that you may acknowledge the truth that from time immemorial even unto eternity the Almighty hath tried, and will continue to try, His servants, so that light may be distinguished from darkness, truth from falsehood, right from wrong, guidance from error, happiness from misery, and roses from thorns.

order.why: Challenge the assumption that religious beginnings received easy acceptance.
Attend to calumny and heedlessness in accounts of earlier messengers.
shortened: Ponder attentively the accounts of the prophets and the Messengers of the past: how it was that they were calumniated against; in what manner they were treated; how it was that individuals became veiled from the Truth and were heedless of the Remembrance of their Lord.

order.why: Keep the named opponents within the source’s religious argument.
shortened: In ancient times, the manifestations of falsehood who stood against the Dawning Places of the All-Merciful had, outwardly, some existence and appearance. Once there was the stubborn Nimrod who was lord of the world. At one time there was the great Pharaoh who was outwardly the philosopher of the Egyptians and renowned among all peoples, ruler of the realm of Egypt and unique among his contemporaries. Once there was the shameless Caiaphas who was chief of the learned ones and the greatest rabbi of the Israelites.

order.why: Read the warning against repeating rejection and mockery.
shortened: Have the tidings not reached you of those who lived before, who denied God's signs and mocked His Messengers, whereupon He seized them with manifest wrath? Fear ye God and reflect upon what hath passed, that ye may be guided in these days when signs descend from every direction.

order.why: Ask what became of those who judged messengers without proof.
shortened: Consider ye and call to mind the generations of old. Where are they who pronounced judgment against Muhammad, the Apostle of God? Where are they who clung to idols, turning away from God, the Lord of all men? Where are they who opposed the Spirit? Where are they who pronounced judgment against God's chosen ones and His messengers without clear proof or explicit Book?

order.why: Retain the concise warning about past conduct and consequence.
shortened: Reflect, then consider the generations of old and what they wrought in their vain life. God seized them for their sins.

order.why: Connect remembered outcomes with deeds.
shortened: Turn not unto the world, but behold the generations of old, for therein lieth a lesson for men of understanding. Each hath attained according to his deeds - among them were those who found a goodly end, and among them were those who found an evil abode.

order.why: Preserve the statement about recurring trials and its attributed saying.
Apply reflection on Christ’s time to present questions.
shortened: Convey my utmost respect to Reverend Mr. Van Kirk and tell him to reflect on past events in the time of Christ so present matters become clear and evident.

order.why: Keep the reported explanation of doubts in former dispensations.
shortened: Verily, if in former dispensations souls harbored doubts, uncertainties and misgivings, it was because they observed that all the divines of the earth would deny and condemn, and none from other nations and peoples would praise even to the extent of a hair's breadth.

order.why: Contrast learned rejection with the response of shepherds.
Distinguish social reputation for knowledge from actual recognition.
Retain the separate contrast of learned exclusion and receptive hearing.
shortened: How many a learned one hath been barred from the Most Great Ocean, and how many an ignorant one hath heard and hastened and partook and drank and said: "Praise be unto Thee, O Thou Who art the Goal of all in the heavens and earth!"

order.why: Consider the image of open doors and sleeping people.
shortened: In the time of Christ, the doors of the divine Kingdom were opened, but the people, being veiled, were negligent and in a deep sleep. Therefore, they were deprived of the spiritual glory.

order.why: Question reliance on ambiguous words without clear explanation.
shortened: Glorified be my Lord, the Most High! Look at the generations of old - did the ambiguous matters, the allegorical verses, and the words they clung to without clear explanation benefit them?

order.why: Ask what prolonged attachment to names has yielded.
Keep the interpretation of Israel and the source’s polemical setting intact.
Read the reported comparison of claims to religious finality.
Preserve the historically specific argument about scripture and authority.
Keep the reported Jeroboam example and its claimed outcome.
shortened: Now these souls who create discord do so in the name of truth - later the result becomes clear. Jeroboam acted in the name of justice and equity, but afterwards the Children of Israel became idol worshippers.

order.why: Retain the reported Arius account and its ocean metaphor.
shortened: Just the same as in the time of Christ. It has retarded the progress of His Cause, as Arius did. One million and a half souls were his followers even the Emperor at Constantinople. Arius was very eloquent. He proved the existence of something that did not exist. But the Ocean of Christ sent forth a wave and cast ashore Arius and all.

order.why: Keep the reported interpretation of Israel’s afflictions attributed.
Read the reported reminder not to repeat earlier regret.
Consider persecution followed by later public admiration.
Let the later significance of the disciples challenge judgments of worth.
shortened: In the time of Christ, outwardly the acceptance of the disciples had no importance - people mocked them, saying "What station or worth do fishermen have?" They ridiculed and laughed at them. But later they understood what importance they had. Later it became clear and they regretted every moment of those times.

order.why: Observe the changing estimation of the Last Supper.
shortened: Do ye not look upon the present, nay rather look ye in the future. The Lord's Supper of His Holiness Christ during the lifetime of that divine Light had no importance in the estimation of the public but consider how the rays of that Sun of Reality illumined that meeting afterward.

order.why: Keep the reported comparison of assemblies with Pentecost.
shortened: "For instance, consider how many a thousand assemblages--religious, political and literary--have been organized in India, Persia, Turkestan, Chinese countries and, in a word, in every part of Asia. All these gave no result except that assemblage of the disciples of Christ on the mount fifty days after Christ's ascension.

order.why: Read the delayed appearance of spiritual stations through stars and daylight.
shortened: During the first century of the holy Manifestations the beginning of the revelation is like the day, because the Sun of Reality is shining upon all the horizons, the stars are invisible. But in the second century, the station and the degree of the sincere ones will become evident. Their lights will become manifest and bright like unto the shining stars. The stations of the apostles of His Holiness Christ became known after three hundred years.

order.why: Notice how remembrance and mourning change after a life has ended.
shortened: Consider in history those noble souls who passed before: after their passing, none mourned them or raised lamentations in their calamity. No eye wept and no heart burned. Yet afterward, behold what mourning occurred and how conditions changed.

order.why: Read the lamp and fire that persecution failed to extinguish.
shortened: They thought that they had done well, that they had extinguished the Lamp, and that they had quenched the Fire which flamed in the tree of Christian certainty; nay, verily, that Lamp hath diffused its dazzling rays unto the Supreme Height and that Fire hath burned until it kindled the hearts of the righteous!"

order.why: Consider the later significance of Mecca.
shortened: You observe that the stony land, because it was the homeland of the Prophet, became the qiblih of the horizons - from all regions they turn toward the Mother of Cities, meaning Mecca, to pray. This was not known in the time of the Prophet, but became apparent afterwards.

order.why: Keep the reported geographical description and pilgrimage comparison.
shortened: In this world there is no soil as unproductive as the soil of Mecca. It is a desert of sand, black, bare mountains and barren sahara. There are no springs in Mecca. They bring in their drinking water from a very remote place. Now because this desert of shifting sand, these fearfully shaped dried mountains, this extremely hot climate became the birthplace of His Holiness Mohamad, the eyes of the Islamic world have turned toward it. Nearly three hundred thousands souls go yearly on a pilgrimage to Mecca to kiss the black sacred stone.

order.why: Read the reported interpretation of the words spoken during migration.
Retain the reported account of changed policy and religious investigation.
shortened: Christianity in France was emancipated in this manner. One of the monarchs in France realized that no matter how many Christians were slain, it bore no fruit. One day he summoned his ministers and consulted [with them]. Thereupon, he announced that he bore no opposition whatsoever to Christianity. This resulted in all the people being enticed to investigate, and gradually they became Christian.
In this Cause, it will also occur likewise.

order.why: Keep the Constantinople anecdote as the source presents it.
Confront the material remnants of armies and conflict.
Ask what mutual violence ultimately achieved.
shortened: Consider the earlier centuries how much the peoples of those times strove, struggled and showed great violence and ferocity, how much blood they shed but ultimately they only uprooted each other and entered the abyss of humiliation and remoteness.

order.why: Read the reported assessment of warfare’s accumulated results.
Uses the historical record of warfare to examine the consequences of prejudice.
Keep the reported criticism of failed peace measures.
Read the account of Alexandria’s bombardment and sudden loss.
Consider the reported consequences of conflict between neighboring powers.
shortened: If the Iranians and Turks had not opposed each other, all these kingdoms would still be under their power today. But they fell into such heedlessness that whenever the Turks were busy with conquests on the European frontiers, the Iranians, seeing them occupied, would attack them, and whenever the Iranians became thus engaged, the Turks would assault them. They gave each other no peace, and every day they pursued pleasure and personal gain and selfish aims until they squandered that glory and laid waste such prosperous realms.

order.why: Keep the reported connection between neglect and defeat.
shortened: The Beloved said:-

"It is evident that negligence from God brings a nation to this path; lack of administration throws people into such defeats. If the Turks were watchful of their interests, a thousand years may have passed without losing any of their domains.

order.why: Read the letter’s examples concerning clerical political intervention.
Preserve the reported incident following the Russian-Iranian war.
shortened: In the Russian-Iranian War, Iran was defeated; and, afterwards, seventy-six of the victors were assigned to settle various affairs and to dispatch the [Iranian] captives to Russia. There was a woman who had two children, whose husband had resisted arrest and avoided being sent [to Russia]. As a result, the Russians kept the wife under surveillance, and, once having discovered her in the public bath, seized her as she emerged. A tremendous commotion broke out in which the entire group of Russians perished.

order.why: Keep the brief report about volunteer military supplies.
shortened: During the time of Abdul Hamid, when volunteer military forces signed up to fight against Russia, each soldier was given a rifle and 200 bullets.

order.why: Examine contradictory wartime announcements in the remembered account.
shortened: During the Russo-Turkish war about 40 years ago, it was announced one day that Russia is defeated. This news created a furor amongst the inhabitants of Acca and on that very evening illuminated all the streets and Bazaars. Next morning it was gravely and greviously given out that the Turkish Commander has been made a prisoner by the Russian Army and they are on their march to Constantinople. The same thing happened three or four years ago during the Turkish-Italian war in Tripoli.

order.why: Place the separate report of censored military news beside it.
Retain the reported chronological oddity in military annals.
Keep the supplied account of disputes over the Persian Gulf.
shortened: Before Shah Abbas, the Dutch seized the Persian Gulf with its seventeen islands belonging to Iran and developed them, taking them completely out of Iran's control.
After much dispute Shah Abbas returned the ships.

order.why: Read the reported division of provinces and tribute.
Keep the short reported example of monarchs and Protestants.
shortened: In the Middle Ages, when the kings of Germany and England were oppressed by the Pope, they would assist the Protestants.

order.why: Retain the account of rival claims to the caliphate.
Read the full historical explanation concerning Acre and the two named rulers.
Keep the separately reported chronology of Acre distinct.
Retain the recorded dates and prophetic interpretation without harmonizing them.
Read the reported strategic importance of Syria.
Keep the reported explanation of names and origins of Acre and Haifa.
shortened: Over the course of history, it has acquired many names. At first it was 'Auk, then became 'akur [Achor] and afterwards 'Akka. The Phoenicians raised this city and their custom was that when they built a town, whatever geometric figure it resembled, they would call it by that name. Since this city was triangular with curved sides, then they called it 'Auk, which had this meaning. Moreover, Haifa was known as Hayfu, meaning 'a town on the skirt of a mountain.'

order.why: Preserve the separate Phoenician account and chronology.
Enter the sacred geography of Acre through the letter’s language.
Keep the reported account of the Holy Land’s religious associations.
shortened: This is the Holy Land from whence all the Prophets and Holy Men came. No country in the world has such a bright light of Religion. The Light of God has always shone upon the world from this land, and the Religion of God has had its Source and Revelation here. It is wonderful even in its physical conformation. The Phoenicians came from here. Their great civilizations spread from Syria. Abraham came to this land. Here His Teaching became known. The King of Salem, Melchizedek, came from this land. All the Prophets had their missions here.

order.why: Retain the short reported praise of those sacred grounds.
